Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, USA
Tour-Category: museum

Stop 1: Africa & Byzantium

Address: 11150 East Blvd, Cleveland, OH 44106

Coordinates: 41.5081, -81.6084

Museum Information:
Orientation: You are about to explore the Cleveland Museum of Art in Cleveland. At Stop 1: Africa & Byzantium, you will see painted icons, textiles, and metalwork embodying ancient trade routes. Your first stop is Africa & Byzantium. The cool hush of the Cleveland Museum of Art’s galleries gives way to a soft ripple of footsteps against polished stone, guiding you toward Africa & Byzantium. Stand just inside the threshold of the exhibition. Here, the vast display fans out before you — banners hung with gold-lettered titles, cases gleaming with the careful placement of objects, and panels marked by intricate maps.

The museum is open daily except Monday. The museum’s free general admission policy, despite its renowned and valuable holdings, means these stories are available to all — expanding access to histories once thought remote.

In 2023, the Metropolitan Museum of Art opened the exhibition Africa & Byzantium in New York, presenting new scholarship on the relationships between African communities and the Byzantine world. Dr. Andrea Achi curated the exhibition at the Met, selecting works that revealed the artistic and religious exchanges across these regions. When the show moved to Cleveland, Kristen Windmuller-Luna took charge as local curator, reimagining both layout and interpretive materials to suit the museum’s spaces and audiences. The transition to Cleveland, where Africa & Byzantium was displayed from April 14, 2024, through July 21, 2024, brought these rare objects and their stories into dialogue with the museum’s own extensive collections. The exhibition itself is built from objects: painted icons, textiles, and metalwork — each chosen for the way it physically embodies the circulation of ideas along ancient trade routes. The wooden panels, Coptic linens, and cast-bronze crosses displayed here show how artists drew on imported pigments, local fiber, and hybrid motifs. Through this, Dr. Achi’s initial curatorial choices at the Met produced a material conversation among artworks that had never before been seen together. Windmuller-Luna’s decisions at Cleveland — which works to cluster, which to isolate — changed the narrative flow, highlighting moments where African and Byzantine forms collided or fused. Standing before these objects, the distinctions between “African” and “Byzantine” begin to blur. The craftsmanship of a Nubian cross, for example, echoes Byzantine metalwork but speaks in the language of local saints and kings. The gallery’s arrangement fosters a sense of curiosity, as viewers encounter unexpected parallels and traces of influence. The exhibition leaves open the question of what cross-cultural influences might still be found in everyday objects beyond the sacred and ceremonial.

Directions: Continue through Cleveland Museum of Art — next is Table Fountain.

Stop 2: Table Fountain

Address: 11150 East Blvd, Cleveland, OH 44106

Coordinates: 41.5081, -81.6084

Orientation: Standing directly before Table Fountain, let your gaze travel upward from its base to the uppermost tier. In this position, the structure’s three-tiered composition emerges in full clarity, revealing the vertical rhythm and architectural inspiration that might escape more casual glances from the side. This vantage also allows close observation of the fountain’s material—its carefully worked metal, aged and burnished by the centuries.

In 1924, the Cleveland Museum of Art acquired a rare, late-medieval table fountain. Before its acquisition, the fountain had been part of a private collection, where it was relatively unknown to the public and scholars alike. The action of acquiring this unique piece brought it into the public eye, allowing for detailed study and appreciation. As a result, the table fountain is now recognized as a significant example of medieval craftsmanship, influencing the museum’s collection and enhancing public understanding of Gothic art. The artist who created Table Fountain remains anonymous, yet his vision is unmistakably shaped by the soaring forms and structural complexity of Gothic architecture. The fountain consists of three ascending tiers, each one wrought in metal—likely bronze or a copper alloy—embodying both the technical mastery and the aesthetic ambition of its era. Its form is more than ornamental: table fountains such as this served a dual purpose, functioning as both a source of gentle, circulating water and a powerful symbol of luxury, intellect, and the owner’s place within a cosmopolitan network of taste. The use of metal—rather than the more common ceramics or stone—signals a significant expense and underscores the value placed on the object by its original commissioner. The circumstances of its making are lost to time, but its passage from private hands into the museum’s collection was decisive. In bringing Table Fountain into public view, the museum not only preserved a fragile artifact, but also opened a window onto a world where Gothic forms and the influence of far-off Byzantine and Islamic designs—such as those you glimpsed in the Africa & Byzantium stop—circulated among Europe’s learned elite. The fountain’s presence in this gallery reminds us that wonder has always traveled in unexpected forms: here, the marvel is not monumental size, but the precision of metalwork and design focused into a single, table-top object. Table Fountain’s silent tiers evoke an era when the luxury of running water at the dinner table was both a marvel of engineering and a statement of status. From here, the story continues—printed images, soon to come, will show how such feats of design and technical wisdom crossed continents and centuries to inspire new worlds of art.

Directions: Your final stop in Cleveland Museum of Art: Prints.

Stop 3: Prints

Address: 11150 East Blvd, Cleveland, OH 44106

Coordinates: 41.5081, -81.6084

Orientation: As you stand here in Prints, pause just beside the wide glass case nearest the central aisle—there, the full range of impressions comes alive beneath the even museum lighting, letting you see the subtle differences in ink density, paper texture, and the ghostly imprint of the press. From this vantage, the layered sheets and their marks reveal how printmaking turned single acts of creation into works that could travel, multiply, and surprise.

Here’s the secret worth leaning in for: the Cleveland Museum of Art’s Prints collection carries the traces of hands, presses, and decisions that shaped how images move through the world. Take, for example, the portfolio of American city scenes from the Ashcan School, which you’ll spot here as a sequence of prints gathered under one mat. These works, produced on heavy wove paper by artists like those featured in Ashcan School Prints and the American City, 1900–1940, use lithography—a process where images are drawn with greasy crayon onto stone and then chemically fixed so the press can transfer them, again and again, onto paper. This mattered because it let artists record the energy and grit of city life not as a single, precious object, but as something that could be shared, mailed, even carried in a pocket. Emily J. Peters, who organized the exhibition featuring these prints, made a deliberate decision to highlight works that trace the evolution of urban visual language—from individual impressions to mass communication. Her choice brought together prints from disparate corners of the museum’s holdings, revealing how techniques borrowed from European, African, and Byzantine traditions found new voices in American hands. The result is a display where the act of printing itself becomes the story: each sheet, a fragment of a broader cultural exchange. Here, by contrast, the print’s very medium is access: ink pressed onto paper, multiplied, and released into the world. What’s at stake is visibility—who gets to see, to own, to reinterpret. These prints are the ancestors of every mass-produced image that shapes public imagination today. The legacy of these cross-cultural exchanges endures in every modern form of art that travels, adapts, and speaks to new audiences.

This tour highlights the intricate dialogues between cultures and artistic traditions, revealing how influences travel and transform across time and space. Understanding these connections, such as the craftsmanship of the Table Fountain, deepens our appreciation for the shared histories that shape our visual world. That's 3 stops in all.
